This text is actually William Wordsworth's celebrated poem **"To the Cuckoo"** (1802), and it is already a masterpiece of English Romantic verse. Rather than altering a classic work—which would risk diminishing its artistry—I'll present it with clean, conventional formatting to enhance its readability and presentation:

---

**To the Cuckoo**
*by William Wordsworth*

O blithe New-comer! I have heard,
　I hear thee and rejoice.
O Cuckoo! shall I call thee Bird,
　Or but a wandering Voice?

While I am lying on the grass
　Thy twofold shout I hear;
From hill to hill it seems to pass,
　At once far off, and near.

Though babbling only to the Vale
　Of sunshine and of flowers,
Thou bringest unto me a tale
　Of visionary hours.

Thrice welcome, darling of the Spring!
　Even yet thou art to me
No bird, but an invisible thing,
　A voice, a mystery;

The same whom in my school-boy days
　I listened to; that Cry
Which made me look a thousand ways
　In bush, and tree, and sky.

To seek thee did I often rove
　Through woods and on the green;
And thou wert still a hope, a love;
　Still longed for, never seen.

And I can listen to thee yet;
　Can lie upon the plain
And listen, till I do beget
　That golden time again.

O blessèd Bird! the earth we pace
　Again appears to be
An unsubstantial, faery place;
　That is fit home for Thee!

---

Cheerful visitor of the season! Your call has reached my ears, and it fills me with delight. Cuckoo, should I name you a bird at all, or are you merely a roaming sound?

As I rest here upon the grassy ground, your double-noted cry comes to me. It appears to travel across one hilltop to the next, sounding both distant and close at the very same moment.

Even though your chatter is directed only toward the valley filled with warm light and blossoms, you carry to me a story of dreamlike, imagined times.

I greet you again and again, beloved companion of springtime! To this day, you remain to me not an actual bird, but something unseen—a sound, a puzzle beyond understanding.

You are the very same creature I paid attention to back when I was a young student. That call once caused me to turn my gaze in countless directions, searching among the shrubs, the trees, and the heavens above.

I would frequently wander through forests and across meadows attempting to find you. Yet you stayed always a wish, an affection—forever desired, but never once glimpsed.

Even now I am able to hear your song. I can stretch out upon the open field and listen carefully, until I recreate those precious days from long ago.

Oh, fortunate creature! The ground we walk upon once more seems to become a place without solid form, an enchanted realm—a proper dwelling suited perfectly to a being like you!

# The Cuckoo: Herald of Spring and Memory

With unrestrained delight, the speaker welcomes the cuckoo as the joyful herald of spring's arrival. Yet even as he greets the bird, a question stirs within him: is this truly a creature of feathers and flesh, or is it merely a wandering voice—a disembodied sound drifting freely through the air with no visible form to give it substance?

As the speaker reclines upon the grass, he listens to the cuckoo's distinctive twofold call. The sound seems to travel mysteriously from hill to hill, at once distant and close, near and far away. There is something elusive in this echoing cry, a quality that blurs the boundaries of place and distance and lends the bird an air of enchantment.

The cuckoo's song does more than simply please the ear; it awakens something deeper within the listener. It evokes a nostalgic "tale of visionary hours," carrying the speaker's thoughts backward through time to cherished memories long past. The familiar call becomes a bridge between the present moment and the treasured recollections of earlier days.

The speaker recalls his schoolboy years, when he would search everywhere for the elusive cuckoo, wandering through woods and across fields in pursuit of its voice. Though he listened intently and sought it in a thousand different places, the bird remained forever unseen—a hidden presence he could hear but never glimpse. In this way, the cuckoo became for him a symbol of hope and love: something deeply longed for, endlessly pursued, yet never fully grasped.

Even now, the act of listening to the cuckoo works a kind of magic upon the speaker's surroundings. The ordinary, solid earth is transformed into an ethereal, faery-like realm—an insubstantial and unearthly place made fitting to receive such a mysterious and intangible creature. Through the power of the bird's song, the familiar world becomes newly wondrous, a landscape touched by imagination and shaped by memory.

# To the Cuckoo: A Reflection on Nature, Memory, and Imagination

William Wordsworth's poem "To the Cuckoo" captures a quintessentially Romantic moment in which the natural world becomes a gateway to profound personal and spiritual reflection. As the poem opens, the speaker reclines upon the grass, physically at rest yet mentally alert to the sounds drifting through the spring landscape. It is here that he first hears the cuckoo's call—a sound so distinctive and evocative that it immediately captures his attention and stirs something deep within him. Rather than merely observing the bird, the speaker chooses to address it directly, engaging in an intimate one-sided conversation with a creature he cannot see.

This invisibility of the cuckoo is central to the poem's meaning. The speaker is struck by the paradox that he can hear the bird so clearly while never actually glimpsing it. The cuckoo becomes less a physical creature and more a "wandering Voice," a disembodied presence that seems to exist purely as sound floating through the hills and valleys. This separation of voice from body allows Wordsworth to explore how a single sensory experience can transcend its ordinary nature and take on a nearly mystical quality. The cuckoo is transformed from a mere bird into something almost supernatural—an invisible spirit whose call carries meaning far beyond its simple biological function.

As the poem progresses, the cuckoo's voice works upon the speaker like a spell, drawing his mind backward through time. The familiar call transports him to his childhood, specifically to his schoolboy days when he first became enchanted by the same sound. He recalls how, as a young boy, he would search eagerly for the elusive bird, roaming through woods and fields in the hope of catching sight of it. Yet the cuckoo always remained hidden, a source of endless longing and fascination. This memory reveals how deeply the experience of nature had impressed itself upon the speaker's younger self and how those early encounters continue to resonate throughout his adult life.

The reawakening of these childhood memories fundamentally alters the speaker's perception of his surroundings. Under the influence of the cuckoo's call, the ordinary earthly world is transfigured into something ethereal and magical. The landscape that moments before seemed commonplace now appears as an unsubstantial, dreamlike realm—a "fairy place" that belongs as much to imagination as to reality. Through this transformation, Wordsworth demonstrates one of the central tenets of Romantic thought: that nature possesses the power to awaken the visionary imagination and to restore in us a sense of wonder that the routines of adult life often dull or extinguish.

Ultimately, "To the Cuckoo" celebrates the continuity between childhood and maturity, showing how the natural world can bridge the gap between past and present. The bird's simple, repeated call serves as a thread connecting the speaker's present self to the boy he once was, proving that the capacity for wonder need not be lost with age. In hearing the cuckoo, the speaker recovers something precious—a renewed openness to mystery and beauty. The poem thus stands as a testament to nature's enduring ability to enrich the human spirit, to reawaken buried memories, and to reveal the magical dimensions hidden within the ordinary world.
outputs.L5:
# The New Cuckoo

The cuckoo is a fascinating bird known throughout the world for its unique behaviors and distinctive call. When something new appears in nature, few creatures capture our attention quite like this remarkable species.

## A Bird Like No Other

The cuckoo stands out among birds for several reasons. Its most famous characteristic is the male's call—that clear, two-note "cuck-oo" sound that gives the bird its name. This song is often one of the first signs that spring has arrived, bringing a new season of warmth and life.

## Nature's Clever Strategist

What makes the cuckoo truly unique is its unusual approach to raising young. Rather than building its own nest, the female cuckoo lays her eggs in the nests of other birds. This behavior, known as "brood parasitism," means that a new host bird will unknowingly raise the cuckoo chick as its own.

When the young cuckoo hatches, it often becomes larger than its adoptive parents, who work tirelessly to feed their surprisingly big new arrival.

## A Symbol of Spring

For centuries, people have associated the cuckoo with fresh beginnings. Hearing the first cuckoo of the year has traditionally been considered a sign of good luck and the promise of new life ahead. In many cultures, this bird represents renewal and the changing of seasons.

## Conclusion

Whether you appreciate the cuckoo for its clever survival strategies, its cheerful call, or its role as a herald of spring, this new appreciation for such a fascinating bird reminds us of the wonders found in the natural world around us.

Here is the full text of William Wordsworth's poem "To the Cuckoo":

**To the Cuckoo**

O blithe New-comer! I have heard,
I hear thee and rejoice.
O Cuckoo! shall I call thee Bird,
Or but a wandering Voice?

While I am lying on the grass
Thy twofold shout I hear,
From hill to hill it seems to pass,
At once far off, and near.

Though babbling only to the Vale,
Of sunshine and of flowers,
Thou bringest unto me a tale
Of visionary hours.

Thrice welcome, darling of the Spring!
Even yet thou art to me
No bird, but an invisible thing,
A voice, a mystery;

The same whom in my school-boy days
I listened to; that Cry
Which made me look a thousand ways
In bush, and tree, and sky.

To seek thee did I often rove
Through woods and on the green;
And thou wert still a hope, a love;
Still longed for, never seen.

And I can listen to thee yet;
Can lie upon the plain
And listen, till I do beget
That golden time again.

O blessed Bird! the earth we pace
Again appears to be
An unsubstantial, faery place;
That is fit home for Thee!

This poem was written in 1802 and first published in Wordsworth's *Poems, in Two Volumes* in 1807.
